title: From physical problems to representation decomposition: step-by-step derivation
description: 44 guided exercises: progress from U(1), unitary matrices, generators, and weight diagrams to physical applications, exact CG coefficients, Racah coefficients, and higher-dimensional four-body recoupling. Each exercise includes hints, a step-by-step derivation, a counterexample, and an independent check, with a linked experiment where available.

exercises.title: U(1) · Why are four phase points not the full continuous group?
exercises.prompt: Generate C₄ from r=i and test whether the 45° phase belongs to this subgroup. Then explain why infinitely many lattice translations can still form a discrete group.
givens: The elements of U(1) are e^(iφ); multiplication adds their phase angles.
Here C₄={1,r,r²,r³}, with r=i. A one-dimensional lattice permits displacements n a, where a>0 and n∈ℤ.
exercises.hint: Calculate the powers through the fourth power, then check how exponents combine modulo 4. For translations, identify the smallest nonzero displacement near the identity.

steps.title: Generate four phase points
steps.explanation: Multiply successive powers of r. The fourth power returns the identity, and the four preceding powers are distinct.

steps.title: Check closure and inverses
steps.explanation: Reduce the sum of exponents modulo 4 to see that every product remains among the four points. Inverses follow by reducing negative exponents modulo 4.

steps.title: Test an angle outside the subgroup
steps.explanation: The 45° phase is (1+i)/√2. Its modulus is 1, but it is not one of the four points. The presence of this element in U(1) does not give a square 45° rotational symmetry.

steps.title: Distinguish infinite from continuous
steps.explanation: There are infinitely many integer translations, yet every nonzero displacement has magnitude at least a. The displacement a/1000 is not a permitted lattice translation, so there are no arbitrarily small nonzero lattice translations near zero.

exercises.answer: C₄={1,i,−1,−i} is a four-element subgroup of U(1). U(1) locally requires one real parameter. The integer lattice-translation group has infinitely many elements but is discrete.
exercises.pitfall: The translation group ℤ is a counterexample to the claim that infinitely many elements imply continuity. Also distinguish the group order 4, the real dimension 1 of U(1), and the size of a chosen representation matrix.

check.question: Which statement is correct?
choices: Infinitely many group elements always imply a continuous group
C₄ is a subgroup of U(1), while infinitely many integer translations can still form a discrete group
U(1) has dimension 1, so it has only one element
check.explanation: Products in C₄ remain among its four points. Integer translations have no arbitrarily small nonzero steps. Dimension counts local parameters, not group elements.

exercises.title: U(2) and SU(2) · What must be checked beyond norm preservation?
exercises.prompt: Determine whether U=diag(e^(−iπ/4),e^(iπ/4)) and V=diag(i,1) belong to U(2) or SU(2). Then use a transformation that mixes basis states to examine what probability conservation means.
givens: U(2) requires M†M=I₂; SU(2) additionally requires det M=1.
A† denotes the conjugate transpose of matrix A, combining transposition with complex conjugation; |↑⟩=(1,0)ᵀ.
exercises.hint: Write the phases as (1∓i)/√2 and take the conjugate transpose entry by entry. A determinant of modulus 1 need not equal 1.

steps.title: Calculate U† and check norm preservation
steps.explanation: The diagonal entries are complex conjugates and each has modulus 1. Multiplying U† by U gives the identity.

steps.title: Check the special condition
steps.explanation: The determinant of U is the product of two conjugate phases, so it is exactly 1.

steps.title: Check the counterexample V
steps.explanation: Each diagonal entry of V also has unit modulus, so V is unitary, but its determinant is not 1.
steps.formula: V†V=I₂ and det V=i≠1, so V∈U(2) but V∉SU(2)

steps.title: Total probability can be preserved while component probabilities change
steps.explanation: Take W=[[1,−1],[1,1]]/√2. Although W belongs to SU(2), it sends the up state to an equal-amplitude superposition. Probabilities for individual basis outcomes can therefore change.

exercises.answer: U belongs to SU(2). V belongs to U(2) but not SU(2). Unitary transformations preserve total probability and inner products while allowing probabilities in a chosen basis to be redistributed.
exercises.pitfall: V is unitary without satisfying the special condition. W preserves total probability while changing the component probabilities. Omitting complex conjugation gives an incorrect unitarity test.

check.question: V=diag(i,1) belong to?
choices: SU(2)
U(2), but not SU(2)
Neither
check.explanation: V†V=I₂, whereas det V=i. Check unitarity and the determinant-one condition separately.

exercises.title: Generators · Why does the same commutator acquire a different factor?
exercises.prompt: Multiply the Pauli matrices to calculate [Tx,Ty], with Ta=σa/2. Then explain what changes when the order is reversed or the σ normalization is used.
givens: [A,B]=AB−BA. This course uses finite transformations U(θ)=exp(−iθT), where T is a Hermitian generator.
exercises.hint: Calculate σxσy and σyσx separately, then subtract. Divide by 4 afterward because each generator contributes a factor of 1/2.

steps.title: Multiply in both orders
steps.explanation: Direct row-by-column multiplication gives two results with opposite signs.

steps.title: Subtract and apply the generator normalization
steps.explanation: The Pauli-matrix commutator is 2iσz. Since Tx and Ty each contain a factor of 1/2, divide this result by 4.

steps.title: Check the commutator and Lie-algebra conventions
steps.explanation: Reversing the order changes the sign. The commutator of Hermitian generators is anti-Hermitian. Taking X=−iT gives the anti-Hermitian Lie-algebra elements used in the mathematical convention.

steps.title: One commuting pair does not make the group Abelian
steps.explanation: In SU(3), T₃ and T₈ commute because they are diagonal, whereas the embedded T₁ and T₂ do not commute.

exercises.answer: [Tx,Ty]=iTz, whereas the σ-matrix convention gives [σx,σy]=2iσz. Exchanging x and y changes the sign. Keep the two normalizations distinct.
exercises.pitfall: The fact that T₃ and T₈ commute does not make SU(3) Abelian. Treating the Hermitian T matrices directly as a real Lie-algebra basis under the ordinary commutator also overlooks the factor of i in this convention.

check.question: With Ta=σa/2, what is [Tx,Ty]?
choices: 2iTz
iTz
check.explanation: The two factors of 1/2 give 1/4. Multiplying [σx,σy]=2iσz by 1/4 gives iσz/2=iTz.

exercises.title: SU(2) · Calculate the Bloch direction from spinor amplitudes
exercises.prompt: Actively rotate a +z spin by 90° about +y. Find the full rotation matrix, final state, z-basis probabilities, and Bloch vector.
givens: U_y(θ)=cos(θ/2)I₂−i sin(θ/2)σy；θ=π/2。
For ψ=(a,b)ᵀ, r=(2Re(a*b),2Im(a*b),|a|²−|b|²), where * denotes complex conjugation.
exercises.hint: Write −iσy as a real matrix, then apply it to the up state. Bloch components are expectation values, not a list made by combining two probabilities with another number.

steps.title: Evaluate the half-angle matrix
steps.explanation: cos(π/4)=sin(π/4)=1/√2, and the nonzero entries of −iσy are −1 and 1.

steps.title: Apply the matrix and check normalization
steps.explanation: The first matrix column gives the final state. Its two amplitudes are equal, and its squared norm remains 1.

steps.title: Calculate the z-basis probabilities
steps.explanation: Each probability is the squared modulus of an amplitude. The amplitude 1/√2 is not itself a probability.

steps.title: Calculate the Bloch vector from the coherence
steps.explanation: The coherence a*b=1/2 is real, and the probabilities are equal. Thus the x component is 1 while y and z are 0, consistent with the right-hand rule.

exercises.answer: Uy(π/2)=[[1,−1],[1,1]]/√2. The final state is (1,1)ᵀ/√2, both z-basis probabilities are 1/2, and the Bloch vector points along +x.
exercises.pitfall: The state ψ₂=(1,i)ᵀ/√2 has exactly the same z-basis probabilities but a Bloch vector along +y. Those two probabilities cannot recover the relative phase or the full direction.

check.question: What is the final Bloch vector in this exercise?
check.explanation: The coherence term 2Re(a*b)=1, while the other two components vanish. Equal probabilities imply rz=0 but do not determine rx and ry.

exercises.title: SU(2) · Make a spinor sign observable as a relative path phase
exercises.prompt: Compare an isolated spin, a two-path interferometer with a rotation on one arm, and a rotation on both arms. Which 2π rotation switches the ideal recombination output ports?
givens: U(n,θ)=cos(θ/2)I₂−i sin(θ/2)n·σ, where n is a unit rotation axis.
The initial state is |+⟩path⊗ψ, with |±⟩path=(|a⟩±|b⟩)/√2 and ψ†ψ=1.
The paths are coherent and have equal amplitudes, with ideal recombination. Apart from the specified spin rotation, there are no additional phases, losses, or decoherence.
exercises.hint: First substitute θ=2π and 4π. Insert the resulting sign into the joint path–spin state, then project onto the ± path basis.

steps.title: Evaluate the 2π and 4π rotations
steps.explanation: The half-angles are π and 2π, and both sine terms vanish. The results hold for every unit rotation axis.

steps.title: Start with an isolated spin
steps.explanation: The two minus signs cancel in ρ=ψψ†, leaving spin probabilities and the Bloch vector unchanged.

steps.title: Apply the 2π rotation only on arm b
steps.explanation: Arm a is unchanged while arm b changes sign, converting the sum of path amplitudes into their difference.

steps.title: Compare output probabilities with a rotation on both arms
steps.explanation: Rotating one arm populates only the − port. Rotating both arms changes the overall sign of the joint state, leaving only the + port populated.
steps.formula: One arm rotated by 2π: P+=0, P−=1; both arms rotated by 2π: P+=1, P−=0

exercises.answer: Under the ideal coherent conditions specified here, a 2π rotation on only one arm switches the output from the + port to the − port. An overall minus sign on an isolated spin, or on both arms together, does not change the readout.
exercises.pitfall: Multiplying both arms by −1 is a counterexample: an overall minus sign does not switch the output port. This exercise tests relative phase; it does not treat time reversal as an ordinary SU(2) rotation.

check.question: After a 2π rotation only on arm b, what is the ideal −-port probability?
check.explanation: The joint state becomes |−⟩path⊗ψ. Its projection onto the − port has squared norm 1, using the equal-amplitude, coherence, and ideal-recombination assumptions of this exercise.

exercises.title: One SU(2) element · How do two-dimensional spinors and three-dimensional vectors differ?
exercises.prompt: Fix the same central element g=−I∈SU(2) and compare its action in the j=1/2 spinor and j=1 vector representations. Explain why matrix size alone cannot identify two groups.
givens: The spin-j irreducible representation of SU(2) has dimension 2j+1, with D^(j)(−I)=(−1)^(2j)I.
Spinors transform as ψ↦Uψ. The action on three-dimensional vectors is defined by U(r·σ)U†=(R(U)r)·σ.
exercises.hint: Substitute the two values of j, then check the conjugation action of −I on the three Pauli directions. A representation can send a nonidentity group element to the identity matrix.

steps.title: Calculate the two representation dimensions
steps.explanation: The same group SU(2) can act on different spaces. The representation label j determines the space's dimension.

steps.title: Evaluate the central element in each representation
steps.explanation: Half-integer and integer j give different signs. I₂ and I₃ act on different spaces and cannot be directly subtracted.

steps.title: Verify the vector action by conjugation
steps.explanation: For a=x,y,z, the factors of −I on the left and right each contribute a minus sign, leaving all three directions unchanged.

steps.title: Explain faithfulness and the induced SO(3) action
steps.explanation: The vector representation identifies the distinct SU(2) elements I and −I, so it is not faithful. Its kernel allows the action to descend to vector rotations in SO(3).

exercises.answer: The same central SU(2) element acts as −I₂ in the spinor representation and I₃ in the j=1 vector representation. Specify the group, its representation space, and the representation's faithfulness separately.
exercises.pitfall: The three-dimensional representation of SU(2) and the fundamental representation of SU(3) both use three-component vectors, but they are not the same group or representation. Their group dimensions are 3 and 8, respectively. The fact that both use 3×3 matrices does not make them identical.

check.question: What represents g=−I in the j=1 representation of SU(2)?
choices: I₃
−I₃
−I₂
check.explanation: In (−1)^(2j), j=1 gives exponent 2 and a positive sign. This representation space has dimension 3.

exercises.title: SU(3) · Eight directions and an embedded two-level rotation
exercises.prompt: Count the independent real parameters of a traceless Hermitian 3×3 matrix. Then use T₁=λ₁/2 to derive the transformation of an initial e₁ state at parameter angles π, 2π, and 4π.
givens: Use the basis e₁=(1,0,0)ᵀ, e₂=(0,1,0)ᵀ, e₃=(0,0,1)ᵀ.
Hermiticity requires real diagonal entries and complex-conjugate pairs of off-diagonal entries. The SU(3) generators must also be traceless.
exercises.hint: Separate the upper-left 2×2 block from the third component. The generator vanishes on that component, so its exponential is always 1. Do not extend the block's −I₂ to −I₃.

steps.title: Count the real parameters
steps.explanation: The diagonal entries give 3 real parameters, and the three complex entries above the diagonal give 6 more. The zero-trace condition removes 1.
steps.formula: 3+2×3=9, 9−1=8; the real dimension of SU(3) is 8

steps.title: Exponentiate the two-level block
steps.explanation: The upper-left block is σx/2, and the generator is zero in the third direction. Separate even and odd powers in the exponential to obtain the full matrix.

steps.title: Apply the matrix to e₁ and set the angle to π
steps.explanation: The first column gives the state at a general angle. At θ=π, only its second component is nonzero.

steps.title: Compare the full matrices at 2π and 4π
steps.explanation: At θ=2π, the first two directions acquire minus signs while the third retains 1. At 4π, all three return to the identity matrix.

exercises.answer: SU(3) has 8 independent real generator directions. T₁ mixes only e₁ and e₂. At π, e₁→−i e₂; at 2π the full matrix is diag(−1,−1,1), and at 4π it returns to I₃.
exercises.pitfall: The determinant of −I₃ is −1, so −I₃ is not in SU(3). The SU(2) result at 2π cannot simply be copied here. Nor does the period of T₁ establish a common period for all SU(3) generators.

check.question: What is the full U₁(2π) for evolution generated by T₁?
choices: I₃
−I₃
check.explanation: The generator eigenvalue of the third basis state is 0, so its exponential is 1. The two mixed components acquire minus signs at 2π, leaving the determinant equal to 1.

exercises.title: SU(3) · Weight differences and phase information missing from the mean
exercises.prompt: Read the fundamental-representation weights from T₃ and T₈, and find the root associated with E₁₂. Then show that evolution under T₃ can change relative phase while leaving the mean weight coordinates unchanged.
givens: Eᵢⱼ has a single nonzero entry, 1 in row i and column j; ψ₀=(e₁+e₂)/√2.
U₃(θ)=exp(−iθT₃). This exercise uses generators Ta=λa/2.
exercises.hint: Weights are simultaneous eigenvalues; a root is the difference between two connected weights. Cartan expectation values of a superposition are probability-weighted means and cannot recover relative phase.

steps.title: Read the three simultaneous eigenvalues
steps.explanation: Read the corresponding entries of the two diagonal matrices in the fixed e₁, e₂, e₃ basis.

steps.title: Calculate the root associated with E₁₂
steps.explanation: E₁₂ maps e₂ to e₁. The difference between left and right multiplication by a diagonal matrix is the eigenvalue difference times E₁₂.

steps.title: Evolve the superposition with a Cartan generator
steps.explanation: The two nonzero components acquire opposite phases, but their probabilities remain 1/2. The Cartan expectation values therefore stay fixed.

steps.title: Check the phase information absent from the mean point
steps.explanation: At θ=π/2, the state is ((1−i)/2,(1+i)/2,0)ᵀ. Comparing the non-Cartan observables T₁ and T₂ reveals the change in their expectation values.

exercises.answer: α₁₂=(1,0). During evolution of ψ₀ under T₃, its mean weight coordinates remain (0,1/(2√3)), while its relative phase and non-Cartan generator expectations change. This mean point is not a new weight of the fundamental representation.
exercises.pitfall: The states at θ=0 and θ=π/2 have the same basis probabilities and Cartan expectation values, but represent different rays. Also distinguish the fundamental representation's 3 weights, the 6 nonzero roots obtained from weight differences, and the 2 zero-weight directions in the adjoint representation.

check.question: What is the root α₁₂ associated with E₁₂?
check.explanation: The root is w₁−w₂: the T₃ eigenvalue difference is 1 and the T₈ difference is 0. The second choice is the superposition's mean point; the third is the root associated with E₁₃.

exercises.title: SU(2) · Derivation of π pulse from exponential matrix
exercises.prompt: Starting from |↑⟩ under resonance conditions, find the time for the first complete transfer to |↓⟩ and interpret the final phase.
givens: H/ℏ=Ωσx/2，Ω>0；σx²=I
exercises.hint: Divide the exponential series into even powers and odd powers. First find the state amplitude, and then take the square of the modulus.

steps.title: Write exponents as trigonometric functions
steps.explanation: Even powers of σx equal I, while odd powers equal σx. The even terms of the exponential series sum to a cosine; the odd terms sum to −i times a sine.

steps.title: acts on the initial state
steps.explanation: Since σx|↑⟩=|↓⟩, the rotation turns one initial basis state into a coherent superposition of two basis states.

steps.title: Find the first probability of one
steps.explanation: First take the square of the absolute value of the state amplitude, and then find the minimum positive time. The sign of the amplitude cannot be used to determine whether the probability is positive or negative.

steps.title: distinguishes state vectors from measurement probabilities
steps.explanation: At this time, the amplitude of the upper state is zero and the amplitude of the lower state is −i. The overall phase alone does not change the measurement probability; if two coherent paths are compared, the relative phase needs to be tracked.

exercises.answer: is tπ=π/Ω, and the final state is −i|↓⟩. This requires the resonance, constant drive, and no decoherence conditions of this problem.
exercises.pitfall: For Δ≠0, the rotation axis is no longer x, and waiting for π/Ω generally does not produce complete inversion.

check.question: Ω=4（ angular frequency unit), what is the time for the first complete transfer?
choices: 4π
check.explanation: is directly substituted into tπ=π/Ω; the time unit is the reciprocal of the used angular frequency unit.

exercises.title: SU(2) · get 1⊗1/2 from highest weight
exercises.prompt: Without using the Clebsch–Gordan coefficients table, find the expansion of |J=3/2,M=1/2⟩ in the |m₁,m₂⟩ product basis.
givens: j₁=1，j₂=1/2；J⃗=j⃗₁+j⃗₂
|3/2,3/2⟩=|1,1/2⟩; respective j labels omitted in product basis
exercises.hint: Apply J−=j₁−+j₂− to the highest-weight state. Evaluate the same action once in the coupled basis and once in the product basis.

steps.title: lists the allowed total angular momentum
steps.explanation: triangle rules allow J=3/2 and J=1/2. The maximum M=3/2 has only one product state, so highest weight states do not need to be mixed.

steps.title: Lower in the coupled basis
steps.explanation: Substitute j=3/2 and m=3/2 into the lowering operator coefficient.

steps.title: Lower in the product basis
steps.explanation: Lowering the first factor has coefficient √2; lowering the second has coefficient 1. The resulting vectors point along orthogonal basis directions.

steps.title: Compare and check normalization
steps.explanation: by √3 to get the change of basis coefficient. The sum of the squares is 2/3+1/3=1, and m₁+m₂ for each term is equal to 1/2.

exercises.answer: |3/2,1/2⟩=√(2/3)|0,1/2⟩+√(1/3)|1,−1/2⟩. Therefore the probability of measuring m₁=0 is 2/3.
exercises.pitfall: A state of definite total J is generally not a state of definite individual m values. CG coefficients are amplitudes; probabilities are their squared absolute values.

check.question: What is the probability of detecting m₁=1 and m₂=−1/2 in the above coupled state?
check.explanation: is √(1/3), and the square of its absolute value is 1/3.

exercises.title: SU(2) · Find the singlet state using lowering operator and orthogonality
exercises.prompt: The M=0 subspace of two spins 1/2 contains two states. Construct the triplet and singlet, and verify that the singlet is not one fixed product state.
exercises.hint: first reduces |↑↑⟩ to obtain a symmetric combination, and then finds a normalized combination orthogonal to it in the M=0 subspace.

steps.title: produces the intermediate component of the triplet state
steps.explanation: |↑↑⟩ of J=1, M=1. lowering operator can act on any factor, so the two items appear with the same sign.

steps.title: Construct orthogonal remaining directions
steps.explanation: In the two-dimensional M=0 subspace, the normalized state orthogonal to the combination of the same sign must take on a relatively negative sign. This lesson takes the positive coefficient of |↑↓⟩.

steps.title: Check the total angular momentum
steps.explanation: The contributions of J+ and J− to both terms cancel each other, while the eigenvalue of Jz is zero. This is consistent with J=0.

steps.title: Check local measurement
steps.explanation: Measuring the first spin's z component gives up or down with probability 1/2 each; the second spin is anticorrelated with it. This is not a single product state with a preselected direction.

exercises.answer: is (|↑↓⟩+|↓↑⟩)/√2, and the singlet state is a relatively negative combination. The latter is invariant under co-rotation and has entanglement .
exercises.pitfall: The "antisymmetry" of the singlet state here only refers to the spin factor; the complete wave function of the same type of electron also includes space and other degrees of freedom.

check.question: What do you get by changing the relative negative sign of the singlet state to a positive sign?
choices: Overall phase change of the same state
The J=1, M=0 triplet component
non-normalized state
check.explanation: Changing the relative sign will change the state. Only when all components multiply by the same phase at the same time is the overall phase change.

exercises.prompt: For two spin 1/2, find the energy of H=κ s⃗₁·s⃗₂ and compare the singlet and triplet states in the energy units of κ=2.
givens: s⃗ is the dimensionless angular momentum, s₁=s₂=1/2
J⃗=s⃗₁+s⃗₂; J=0 or 1; κ has energy unit
exercises.hint: Expand J⃗² and rewrite the dot product into a combination of three Casimir operator .

steps.title: expanded total angular momentum squared
steps.explanation: The operators of the two factors commute each other, so the cross term is twice the dot product.

steps.title: Substitute the eigenvalues of each subspace
steps.explanation: The squared eigenvalue of each spin 1/2 is 3/4, and the total squared eigenvalue is J(J+1).

steps.title: calculates J=0 and J=1 respectively

steps.title: Find the difference and interpret the symbols

triplet state

exercises.title: SU(3) · Check 27-dimensional representation from Dynkin tags
exercises.prompt: Find the dimension, conjugate label and quadratic Casimir of (p,q)=(2,2), and determine whether these numbers are energies.
givens: C₂(p,q)=[p²+q²+pq+3p+3q]/3
uses the normalization of Tₐ=λₐ/2; the conjugation labels are (q,p)
exercises.hint: Calculate the dimension and Casimir separately and do not confuse them with the dimension of the group itself.

steps.title: Find the dimension of the representation space
steps.explanation: The three factors are 3, 3, and 6; divide their product by 2. The resulting number counts independent states in the representation space.

steps.title: Find the quadratic Casimir
steps.explanation: Add the square term, mixed term, and linear term separately, and the sum is 24.

steps.title: Check conjugation
steps.explanation: still gets (2,2) after swapping p and q, so this representation is equivalent to its own conjugate.

steps.title: gives the result the correct physical meaning
steps.explanation: 27 is representation dimension and 8 is this normalized Casimir eigenvalue; neither gives the energy directly. If a model also has H=aC₂+bI, the energy can be calculated from its coefficients.
steps.formula: E=8a+b only when H=aC₂+bI is given

exercises.answer: (2,2) is the 27-dimensional representation of the self-conjugate, C₂=8. The real dimension of the SU(3) group is still 8, which is exactly the same as the Casimir value here is just a numerical coincidence of different concepts.
exercises.pitfall: The same conjugation label indicates self-conjugation; conversely, it cannot be assumed that two representations are equivalent just because they have the same dimensions.

check.question: Both 3 and 3̄ have quadratic Casimir 4/3. What does this imply?
choices: They must be equivalent representations
quadratic Casimir cannot distinguish between these two representations on its own
They are all four-dimensional representations
check.explanation: label (1,0) is different from (0,1); quadratic Casimir is invariant under p,q exchange.

exercises.title: SU(3) · Derivation of 3⊗3̄ from the trace of the matrix
exercises.prompt: Identify 3⊗3̄ with the space of complex 3×3 matrices. Prove that it contains a singlet and find the dimension of the remaining subspace.
givens: M→UMU†，U∈SU(3)
Tr(UMU†)=Tr M；UIU†=I
matrix space is 3×3=9
exercises.hint: Split an arbitrary matrix into a multiple of the identity and a traceless part.

steps.title: Isolate the invariant direction
steps.explanation: identity matrix direction is invariant under all conjugate transformations, so this dimensional space is trivial representation .

steps.title: Construct the traceless part
steps.explanation: subtracts the trace direction to get M₀. The conjugate transformation still keeps its trace zero, so this eight-dimensional subspace is closed to the group action.

steps.title: Identify the adjoint representation
steps.explanation: The conjugation action on traceless matrices is the complexified adjoint representation, of dimension 9−1=8. The original tensor-product space therefore splits into 1 and 8.

steps.title: Normalize singlets and interpret indicators
